814	 Discussion
815	
816	The aim of this study was to assess the effectiveness of a secondary injury prevention intervention in a
817	
818	systems-based approach for the early detection and management of HSI and time-loss groin injuries
819	
820	within an Australian male professional football club. A key finding of this study was that HSI and time-
821	
822	loss groin injury burdens were reduced during the intervention period when compared with the control
823	
824	period. Following the detection of subclinical forms of injury via greater screening and monitoring
825	
826	practices, a cascade of indicated interventions shows preliminary positive evidence in reducing the
827	
828	severity of HSI, albeit non-significantly. Forwards and wide positions within the intervention period
829	
830

832	were more prone to post-match isometric strength reduction alerts compared with central positions. This
833

836

846	
847	literature of similar methodology.6 A notable difference between our current study and the previous

852

 Player workload management

Player workload was individually monitored throughout the season by the team strength and

conditioning coach and sport scientist, with a standardised monitoring protocol utilised across both

reporting periods. All monitoring data were recorded using password protected athlete monitoring

software (Athlete Monitoring, Moncton, Canada), with player training status reviewed daily across both

reporting periods. Workload was quantified using both internal and external load measures and was

collected for all field and strength training sessions (inclusive of recovery/rehabilitation sessions) and

match-play (friendly and competitive). Global positioning system (GPS) data was used to quantify


                                                             oo
external load measures across all field sessions with monitored variables including total distance, and

                                                               f
distances covered at specific thresholds, namely high-speed distance (>19.8 km.h-1), and sprinting


                                             re

                                                -p
rating of perceived exertion (sRPE) method23 which has been validated in football.24 In addition, players
                                                   r

                                    lP

Injury definition and data collection

            Jo
An injury was defined as any physical complaint resulting from a football match or training leading to

the player being unable to fully participate in future matches or training (time-loss definition).25 As

such, both acute and longstanding groin injuries were encompassed within this definition. All injury

assessments were performed by the team physiotherapist and/or sports physician and a player was

considered injured until they were cleared to be available for match selection. Injuries were categorised

by severity and classified as being either: minimal (1 - 3 days absence from training and/or match-play),

mild (4 – 7 days absence), moderate (8 – 28 days absence) or severe (greater than 28 days absence).26

The surveillance period for the study included both the pre-season and in-season, inclusive of all

matches and training sessions. If a player was injured at the end of the season, a return-to-play date was

estimated based on all available evidence.25 All data collection protocols and data reporting adhered to



                                                                                                        9
 the consensus statement on injury definitions and data collection procedures in studies of football

injuries.25



Statistical analysis

Normality of the data was assessed using the Shapiro-Wilk test and visually via Q-Q plots. Welch’s t-

test for independent samples, equal variances not assumed, was used for parametric data (age, height,

and mass), while Mann-Whitney U test was used for non-parametric data (weekly training sessions,

weekly matches) to investigate differences between the control and intervention periods.27 Effect sizes


                                                            oo
were calculated using Hedges g for parametric data and the rank-biserial correlation r for non-

parametric data.27                                            f
                                            re -p
Poisson regression was used to analyse injury incidence rates (IIRs) with the number of observed
                                                  r
injuries as the response variable, cohort period as an independent variable and exposure as an offset. A

                                   lP
dispersion test from the ‘AER’ package28 was used to test the null hypothesis of equidispersion of the

response variable.29 A quasi-Poisson or negative binomial regression model was used instead where the
                       urna
assumption of equidispersion was not met. The potential confounding effects of age, height, and mass

on the response variable was also explored. Overall, match and training IIRs are reported as the number

              Jo
of injuries per 1000 player hours ((∑ injuries/ ∑ exposure hours) x 1000). Injury burden is reported

as days absence per 1000 player hours (injury incidence x mean severity). IIRs and rate ratios (RRs)

are reported with corresponding 95% CI, with intervals that did not include 1.0 indicating statistical

significance. All analyses were conducted using the statistical software R (Version 4.1.0).30

(5 dominant and 13 non-dominant) and 8 time-loss groin injuries (3 dominant and 5 non-dominant) in

the intervention group. No adverse events or injuries occurred as a result of strength testing in either

the control or intervention periods.

                                                                                                              14
 Discussion

The aim of this study was to assess the effectiveness of a secondary injury prevention intervention in a

systems-based approach for the early detection and management of HSI and time-loss groin injuries

within an Australian male professional football club. A key finding of this study was that HSI and time-

loss groin injury burdens were reduced during the intervention period when compared with the control

period. Following the detection of subclinical forms of injury via greater screening and monitoring

practices, a cascade of indicated interventions shows preliminary positive evidence in reducing the

severity of HSI, albeit non-significantly. Forwards and wide positions within the intervention period


                                                             oo
were more prone to post-match isometric strength reduction alerts compared with central positions. This

                                                               f
highlights the potential for individual and position-based modifications to subsequent training sessions


                                             re
in the post-match period as part of a secondary injury prevention system.

                                                -p r
Adhering to the system parameters outlined in Figure 1, a reduction in the burdens of both HSI and

                                    lP
time-loss groin injury in male professional football players was observed, replicating results in the

literature of similar methodology.6 A notable difference between our current study and the previous
                    urna
study is the level of competition and the instability of coaching staff during these periods. Previously,

a novel HSI prevention system incorporating secondary prevention in addition to usual care (primary

             Jo
and tertiary prevention) was able to lower HSI burden in youth football players (12.9 days absence/1000

h (90.8%) decrease) when compared to usual care only (intervention period: 1.3 days absence/1000 h;

control period: 14.2 days absence/1000 h).6 While similarly, an early detection and management

strategy for the monitoring of hip and groin strength was able to reduce in-season hip and groin injury

burden when compared to pre-season (mean difference: -5.97 days absence; 95% CI [-11.27, -0.66]).7

It must be noted both studies were completed in youth football thus limiting the applicability to our

current study. Nevertheless, the implementation of early detection and indicated interventions alongside

primary and tertiary injury prevention shows promise in reducing HSI and time-loss groin injury

burdens.




                                                                                                      15
 We identified post-match isometric strength reduction trends which may be of value for practitioners in

the context of post-match monitoring and subsequent training prescription. Dominant limbs in our study

were more likely to have strength reductions than non-dominant limbs during testing two days post-

match (≥40 h). This is consistent with previous research in which post-match non-dominant isometric

hamstring strength (90o knee flexion) recovers quicker than that of dominant, with suggested links to a

higher frequency of technical actions (long passes and shots) performed using the dominant limb.31 We

also observed over a third of all strength reduction alerts to involve ‘forwards’, while wide positions

(wide midfielders and wide defenders) were more prone to alerts than central positions (central


                                                             oo
defenders and central midfielders). This may be attributed to forward and wide positions completing a

                                                               f
greater number of sprints and total sprint distance (p < 0.001) during match-play compared with central


                                             re
positions.22 Together these findings provide practitioners with relevant information to inform individual

                                                -p
and position-based modifications to subsequent training sessions in the post-match period as part of a

secondary injury prevention system.                r
                                    lP
                    ur
While the results of the present study suggest the introduction of secondary injury prevention within


                      na
male professional football may be useful to clubs, we refrain from advocating their use in isolation.

Recent study has shown repeated strength testing as a means of monitoring has limited predictive value

            Jo
for HSI,32 while there is limited evidence to support primary prevention exercise-based strategies alone

in preventing muscle injury in elite football.5 Instead, complementing the various pathology-based

(primary, secondary, and tertiary prevention) and risk factor-based (universal, selective and indicated)

injury prevention categorisations via an integrated systems-based approach is recommended.6,7,33

Despite these recommendations, there was no statistically significant evidence to suggest the daily

bilateral hip adductor squeeze peak force and hamstring (sit-and-reach) flexibility testing in the control

period failed to provide valuable insights to assist in reducing injury burden when compared to in-

season post-match testing within a secondary prevention systems-based approach.



A strength of this study is that it was undertaken within a male professional football club over multiple

seasons. The real-world application of the utilised injury prevention framework suggests its

                                                                                                       16
 implementation elsewhere is realistic and feasible. The test protocols are quick to administer, acceptable

to players and coaching staff and may be implemented in-season without interference to team schedules

or causing injury. Interventions are individualised and may be particularly pertinent during congested

match schedules. However, there are limitations to be noted within this study. We saw an increase,

albeit not statistically significant, in HSI incidence in the intervention period compared with the control

period. This increase in incidence may be due to a concept termed the ‘lead time problem’ where the

practice of increased screening and monitoring practices leads to a greater number of cases being

identified.8 Despite this increase in incidence, the early identification of injuries enabled the expedited


                                                              oo
application of indicated interventions to reduce injury severity and burden and to subsequently increase

                                                                f
player availability, which is linked to positive performance outcomes in football.34


                                              re -p
Due to the nature of professional sport, staffing changes across the study period were inevitable. There
                                                    r
were four head coach, two physiotherapist and two strength and conditioning coach changes across our

                                     lP
five-season study period. Due to this instability, internal relationships and communication quality



                     ur
between the coaching staff may have been affected. This is particularly relevant given high


                       na
communication quality between the medical team and head coach is associated with low injury burden,

low incidence of severe injuries, high training attendance and high match availability.35 Similarly,

            Jo
different coaching leadership styles have been proven to affect injury rates and player availability, with

a negative correlation between the overall level of transformational leadership of the head coach and

the incidence of severe injuries.36 While attributing causation is beyond the scope of our study, the effect

of coaching and medical staff instability is unknown, yet is likely to have contributed to the difference

in the outcome during periods of transition.35,36 As staffing changes are frequent in professional football,

this further supports the need for solid monitoring systems to help mitigate the influence of changing

staff profiles on player injury incidence and burden rates.



Results must also be considered with the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic in mind. There was an

increase in training injury burdens for HSI and time-loss groin injuries during the intervention period

(encompassing the restart to the 2019/2020 season following a three-month cessation of all team-based

                                                                                                         17
 activity due to COVID-19) compared with the control period. Recent research supports this trend, with

spikes identified in training injury burdens37 with links to short-term detraining effects due to

quarantine/periods of inactivity.38 Similarly, due to season schedule changes stemming from COVID-

19, there was a reduced pre-season for the 2020/21 season, with 65 days available for pre-season

training compared with a mean of 109 days from the preceding four seasons. This is particularly

pertinent given an increase of 10 pre-season sessions is linked with a decrease in severe injury incidence

(-0.20 severe injuries/1000 h) and injury burden (-21.8 layoff days/1000 h).39 Despite an increase in

training injury burdens linked to the COVID-19 pandemic, overall HSI and time-loss groin injury


                                                              oo
burdens were still reduced in the intervention period when compared with the control period.

                                                                f
                                              re
Finally, a non-randomised study design reduces the strength of the results obtained in the present study,

                                                 -p
which must be considered when interpreting the practical implications of this research. Despite a five-
                                                    r
season monitoring period, the relative strength of the study was also restricted by a sample size limited

                                     lP
to 21 – 31 players per season pertaining to one club only. The ability to generalise results outside of this



                     ur
specific context is therefore limited. A risk of confirmation bias may also have been present within this


                       na
study. Given the distinction between end of time loss and return to play is not objectively clear, 40 the

possibility of sports medicine staff subconsciously influencing return to play decision making of injured

             Jo
players to improve the effectiveness of the intervention must also be considered.



Conclusion

The implementation of a systems-based secondary injury prevention intervention provides preliminary

positive findings in reducing HSI and time-loss groin injury burdens in a cohort of male professional

football players, when compared with a control period. This study provides practitioners with a practical

framework that can be applied in male professional football, that is acceptable to players and coaches,

without interfering with normal team schedules.




                                                                                                         18
 Acknowledgements

The authors would like to thank all the players of the team considered in the study for their help and

cooperation. This research was supported by an Australian Government Research Training Program

(RTP Scholarship).



Declaration of Interests

No potential conflict of interest was reported by the author(s).

Strength and Conditioning Journal. 2023.",
   "doi":"",
   "abstract":"The countermovement jump (CMJ) is one of the most used performance assessments in strength and conditioning. The article discusses how the metrics selected from CMJ testing may differ when the test is used as a proxy for athletic performance, as part of neuromuscular fatigue monitoring, or as part of a test battery for return to performance in injured athletes.",
   "tldr":"The metrics worth tracking from a countermovement jump depend on why the test is being used. Jump height and peak power track strength and speed well but respond poorly to fatigue, so time-based metrics are often more useful for fatigue monitoring.",
   "methods":"Narrative review of published CMJ studies on associations with strength, speed and change of direction, fatigue sensitivity and injury rehabilitation, with a proposed framework (Figure 1) for metric selection. No systematic search is described. Worked examples use hypothetical group and individual data to show how the coefficient of variation can set the threshold for real change.",
   "findings":"Jump height and peak power were consistently associated with strength, linear speed and change of direction in the cited studies. In a meta-analysis of 151 fatigue studies (63 CMJ metrics), maximal jump height and peak power were not sensitive to fatigue (ES -0.04 each), whereas time-based metrics such as time to take-off and flight time:contraction time ratio changed more over 24 to 72 hours. In a cited snowboard cross study, acute fatigue reduced absolute peak force (ES -2.15) and increased the time measures. Worked example: a 2.9% change in jump height was smaller than the 3.8% CV, so it cannot be called real, while a 6.2% change in time to take-off was larger than its 4.2% CV.",
   "limitations":"The review does not describe how studies were searched or selected, and it relies on the authors' anecdotal experience for parts of the framework. Many correlations are drawn from different populations and tests, and the worked examples are explicitly hypothetical. The article focuses on kinetic data from a force plate and does not weigh video or kinematic measures. The article's own DOI is not printed in the text.",
   "practicalImplications":"Choose CMJ metrics according to the purpose of testing: outcome metrics such as jump height, force and power for performance profiling, time-based metrics and RSI-modified for fatigue monitoring, and landing force and inter-limb asymmetry for rehabilitation. Before reading a change as real, compare it with the metric's own coefficient of variation, measured by test-retest, using group or individual thresholds.",
   "athleteDev":"For performance profiling, CMJ height, force and power link to strength, sprint and change of direction measures and can be used as proxies. For a squad, check whether a change exceeds each metric's own test-retest variation before acting on it.",
   "rtp":"The article only briefly covers injured athletes and does not validate any return-to-sport threshold. It suggests landing force and asymmetry measures may show residual deficits better than jump height or power, but it cannot be used to set return-to-play criteria."
 }
}

   "tldr":"The metrics worth tracking from a countermovement jump depend on why the test is being used. Jump height and peak power track strength and speed well but respond poorly to fatigue, so time-based metrics are often more useful for fatigue monitoring.",
   "methods":"Narrative review of published CMJ studies on associations with strength, speed and change of direction, fatigue sensitivity and injury rehabilitation, with a proposed framework (Figure 1) for metric selection. No systematic search is described. Worked examples use hypothetical group and individual data to show how the coefficient of variation can set the threshold for real change.",
   "findings":"Jump height and peak power were consistently associated with strength, linear speed and change of direction in the cited studies. In a cited snowboard cross study, acute fatigue reduced absolute peak force (ES -2.15) and increased the time measures. 20	                                    Background: Outcomes after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) are highly variable. Previous studies have
21	                                    failed to report the relationship between fear, objective measures of function, and reinjury rates. The purpose of this study
22	                                    was to determine whether fear was related to functional performance measures and risk of second ACL injury after ACLR
23	                                    and return to sport (RTS).
24	                                    Hypothesis: Fear will be associated with performance on functional testing and second ACL injury rate.
25	                                    Study Design: Prospective cohort study.
26	                                    Level of Evidence: Level 2.
27	                                    Methods: A total of 40 patients cleared to RTS after ACLR completed the Tampa Scale of Kinesiophobia (TSK-11), hop
28	                                    testing, and quadriceps strength testing, bilaterally. Patients were tracked for 12 months after RTS to identify the incidence of
29	                                    second ACL injury. Chi-square analyses determined whether patients with high fear (TSK-11, ≥17) were more likely to have
30	                                    lower levels of activity, greater asymmetry on functional testing, and higher reinjury rates.
31	                                    Results: Patients with greater fear on the TSK-11 (≥17) at RTS were 4 times (odds ratio [OR], 3.73; 95% CI, 0.98-14.23) more
32	                                    likely to report lower levels of activity, 7 times (OR, 7.1; 95% CI, 1.5-33.0) more likely to have a hop limb symmetry lower
33	                                    than 95%, and 6 times (OR, 6.0; 95% CI, 1.3-27.8) more likely to have quadriceps strength symmetry lower than
34	                                    90%. Patients who went on to suffer an ipsilateral second ACL injury had a greater TSK-11 score at the time of RTS (mean,
35	                                    19.8 ± 4.0) than those who did not suffer a second ACL injury (mean, 16.4 ± 3.6) (P = 0.03). Patients with a TSK-11 score of
36	                                    19 or greater at the time of RTS were 13 times (relative risk, 13.0; 95% CI, 2.1-81.0) more likely to suffer a second ACL tear
37	                                    within 24 months after RTS.
38	                                    Conclusion: Patients with greater self-reported fear were less active, presented with lower single-leg hop performance and
39	                                    isometric quadriceps strength, and had an increased risk of suffering a second ACL injury in the 24 months after RTS.
40	                                    Clinical Relevance: Self-reported fear of movement/reinjury after ACLR at the time of RTS may be an important measure
41	                                    to incorporate into discharge criteria prior to release to return to pivoting and cutting sports after ACLR.
42	                                    Keywords: ACL reconstruction; second injury; fear; functional performance

                                    Self-Reported Fear Predicts Functional
                                    Performance and Second ACL Injury
                                    After ACL Reconstruction and Return
                                    to Sport: A Pilot Study
                                    Mark V. Paterno, PT, PhD, MBA, SCS,*† Kaitlyn Flynn, DPT, SCS,‡ Staci Thomas, MS,§
                                    and Laura C. Schmitt, PT, PhD||

                                    Background: Outcomes after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) are highly variable. Previous studies have
                                    failed to report the relationship between fear, objective measures of function, and reinjury rates. The purpose of this study
                                    was to determine whether fear was related to functional performance measures and risk of second ACL injury after ACLR
                                    and return to sport (RTS).
                                    Hypothesis: Fear will be associated with performance on functional testing and second ACL injury rate.
                                    Study Design: Prospective cohort study.
                                    Level of Evidence: Level 2.
                                    Methods: A total of 40 patients cleared to RTS after ACLR completed the Tampa Scale of Kinesiophobia (TSK-11), hop
                                    testing, and quadriceps strength testing, bilaterally. Patients were tracked for 12 months after RTS to identify the incidence of
                                    second ACL injury. Chi-square analyses determined whether patients with high fear (TSK-11, ≥17) were more likely to have
                                    lower levels of activity, greater asymmetry on functional testing, and higher reinjury rates.
                                    Results: Patients with greater fear on the TSK-11 (≥17) at RTS were 4 times (odds ratio [OR], 3.73; 95% CI, 0.98-14.23) more
                                    likely to report lower levels of activity, 7 times (OR, 7.1; 95% CI, 1.5-33.0) more likely to have a hop limb symmetry lower
                                    than 95%, and 6 times (OR, 6.0; 95% CI, 1.3-27.8) more likely to have quadriceps strength symmetry lower than
                                    90%. Patients who went on to suffer an ipsilateral second ACL injury had a greater TSK-11 score at the time of RTS (mean,
                                    19.8 ± 4.0) than those who did not suffer a second ACL injury (mean, 16.4 ± 3.6) (P = 0.03). Patients with a TSK-11 score of
                                    19 or greater at the time of RTS were 13 times (relative risk, 13.0; 95% CI, 2.1-81.0) more likely to suffer a second ACL tear
                                    within 24 months after RTS.
                                    Conclusion: Patients with greater self-reported fear were less active, presented with lower single-leg hop performance and
                                    isometric quadriceps strength, and had an increased risk of suffering a second ACL injury in the 24 months after RTS.
                                    Clinical Relevance: Self-reported fear of movement/reinjury after ACLR at the time of RTS may be an important measure
                                    to incorporate into discharge criteria prior to release to return to pivoting and cutting sports after ACLR.
                                    Keywords: ACL reconstruction; second injury; fear; functional performance

 "domains":["Rehabilitation & Return to Sport","Brain Health & Psychology","Sports Medicine & Injury"],
 "audiences":["Rehabilitation","Sports Medicine","Athletic Training"],
 "sports":["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations":["Injured Athletes","Youth / Adolescent"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Prospective cohort pilot of 40 patients (ages 10 to 25, mean 16.2) cleared for return to sport after primary ACL reconstruction, who completed the TSK-11 fear questionnaire, the Marx activity scale, single-leg hop tests and isometric quadriceps strength, and were followed for 24 months. Patients with TSK-11 of 17 or more (n = 19) more often had low Marx activity (73.7% vs 42.9%), hop limb symmetry index of 95% or less (55.6% vs 15%) and quadriceps LSI of 90% or less (50% vs 14.3%) than low-fear patients. Fifteen patients (37.5%) had a second ACL injury, and ipsilateral injury was linked to higher TSK-11 scores (19.8 vs 16.4, P = 0.03).",
 "screeningLimitations":"The study is a 40-patient pilot at one institution, with 8 ipsilateral and 7 contralateral second injuries, so the injury estimates are very imprecise. The activity CI crosses 1 (OR 3.73, 95% CI 0.98 to 14.23), the cut-offs were chosen from clinical convention, and the associations are not causal.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could treat the TSK-11 as a validated discharge gate that predicts reinjury, when this pilot found associations in 40 patients and the authors say it needs further study before it is used as a criterion.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2017,
   "citation":"Paterno MV, Flynn K, Thomas S, Schmitt LC. Self-Reported Fear Predicts Functional Performance and Second ACL Injury After ACL Reconstruction and Return to Sport: A Pilot Study. Sports Health. 2017.",
   "doi":"10.1177/1941738117745806",
   "abstract":"Prospective cohort pilot of 40 patients cleared to return to sport after ACL reconstruction. Fear was measured with the TSK-11 at return to sport and compared with activity level, single-leg hop and quadriceps limb symmetry, and second ACL injury over 24 months. High-fear patients (TSK-11 of 17 or more) were more likely to have lower activity and hop and quadriceps asymmetry. A TSK-11 score of 19 or more was associated with a higher risk of second ACL tear within 24 months.",
   "tldr":"Athletes returning from ACL reconstruction who reported high fear at clearance were less active, had more hop and quadriceps asymmetry, and had more second ACL injuries. The paper suggests fear may belong in discharge criteria, but this 40-patient pilot cannot set a release threshold.",
   "methods":"Forty patients aged 10 to 25 who had been cleared to return to pivoting and cutting sports after primary ACL reconstruction were tested within four weeks of clearance. Testing included the TSK-11, the Marx Activity Rating Scale, four single-leg hop tests and isometric quadriceps strength on a Biodex dynamometer. Patients were split at a TSK-11 score of 17, and second ACL injuries were tracked for 24 months with chi-square analysis.",
   "findings":"High-fear patients (n = 19) had lower Marx activity in 73.7% versus 42.9% of low-fear patients (OR 3.73, 95% CI 0.98 to 14.23), hop LSI of 95% or less in 55.6% versus 15% (OR 7.1, 95% CI 1.5 to 33.0), and quadriceps LSI of 90% or less in 50% versus 14.3% (OR 6.0, 95% CI 1.3 to 27.8). Fifteen patients (37.5%) had a second ACL injury; the ipsilateral group had higher TSK-11 scores than those without (19.8 vs 16.4, P = 0.03), and a score of 19 or more had RR 13.0 (95% CI 2.1 to 81.0). The TSK-11 had an AUC of 0.740 for ipsilateral injury, with sensitivity 0.75 and specificity 0.81. TSK-11 was not associated with contralateral injury (P = 0.652).",
   "limitations":"Only 40 patients from one institution, a pilot study with very few ipsilateral (8) and contralateral (7) injuries, so the RR and AUC are unstable. The activity association is not statistically clear (CI crosses 1), and the 90% and 95% LSI cut-offs are debated. The population was young and active athletes planning to return to cutting and pivoting sports, and the authors did not control rehabilitation or surgeon return-to-sport criteria.",
   "practicalImplications":"Asking athletes to complete the TSK-11 at clearance is quick and may flag those with higher fear who also show asymmetry or lower activity. The authors suggest fear may be worth considering in discharge planning, alongside hop and strength tests, but they do not give a validated cut-off for release.",
   "athleteDev":"Fear scores at return to sport may help identify athletes who are less likely to return to high activity levels. The data are not enough to change the training plan for an individual athlete.",
   "rtp":"The paper directly informs return-to-sport decisions by suggesting that fear at clearance may be a discharge criterion for pivoting and cutting sports. The authors say this needs further study, and the study cannot establish a causal link or set a score that clears an athlete."
 }
}

 "evidenceSummary":"Cross-sectional video review of 251 NFL injury plays from the 2017 season, 211 with a diagnosed sport-related concussion (SRC) and 40 without, scored independently by two expert raters using an AFL visible-signs checklist. Slow to get up was the most frequent sign in concussed players (65.9% averaged across raters), and about 26% of concussed players showed no visible sign. The checklist as a whole had sensitivity of 73% and specificity of 65% (AUC 0.66, which the authors classify as poor), and motor incoordination and loss of responsiveness were the only signs that remained significant in multivariate analysis.",

 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read a high-specificity sign, such as motor incoordination or loss of responsiveness, as enough to diagnose concussion, when the authors state that the diagnosis cannot be made from visible signs alone and that a multimodal sideline evaluation is required.",

   "year":2020,
   "citation":"Elbin RJ, Zuckerman SL, Sills AK, Crandall JR, Lessley DJ, Solomon GS. Sensitivity and Specificity of On-Field Visible Signs of Concussion in the National Football League. Neurosurgery. 2020.",
   "doi":"10.1093/neuros/nyaa072",
   "abstract":"Video review by two expert raters of 251 NFL injury plays from the 2017 season (211 diagnosed with sport-related concussion, 40 not) using a visible-signs checklist. Slow to get up and motor incoordination were the most frequent and sensitive signs, and 26% of concussed players showed no visible sign. The checklist had sensitivity of 73%, specificity of 65% and an AUC of 0.66, which the authors call poor, so concussion cannot be diagnosed from visible signs alone.",
   "tldr":"In NFL video review, the visible-signs checklist missed about a quarter of diagnosed concussions and had poor overall discrimination (AUC 0.66). Visible signs are one part of the sideline evaluation, not a diagnostic tool on their own.",
   "methods":"Prospective observational cross-sectional study using video of injury plays from the 2017 NFL season where a player was removed for suspected concussion. Two expert raters independently scored the AFL visible-signs checklist for each play. Logistic regression tested each sign, and a receiver operating characteristic curve with AUC summarised the checklist. Sensitivity and specificity were calculated against the team physician and neurotrauma consultant's diagnosis.",
   "findings":"Concussed players most often showed slow to get up (averaged 65.9%) and motor incoordination (28.4%). In non-concussed players, slow to get up was also most common (60.0%). The checklist had combined sensitivity of 73.46% and specificity of 65.0%, and 26% of concussed players showed no visible sign. Multivariate logistic regression identified motor incoordination (OR 3.96, 95% CI 1.64 to 9.56, P = .002) and loss of responsiveness (OR 5.17, 95% CI 1.14 to 23.42, P = .033) as significant predictors. The AUC was 0.66.",
   "limitations":"Two raters, with no third rater to resolve disagreements; only one season; only players removed for suspected concussion were reviewed; and a league-specific checklist. The Discussion states sensitivity and specificity of 76% and 63%, but the Results and Table 5 give 73% and 65%, so the Discussion figures should not be quoted. The sign definitions differ from the new consensus list, and the authors note the diagnosis is multimodal.",
   "practicalImplications":"Use visible-sign checks as one input to a full sideline or acute evaluation, not as a stand-alone screen. Signs with high specificity, such as loss of responsiveness, may still support removal from play, but a 1 in 4 miss rate means no sign should clear a player to continue.",
   "athleteDev":"Not applicable to performance development. The paper is about recognising concussion in games.",
   "rtp":"The paper does not inform return to sport. It addresses identification of concussion at the time of injury, and the authors do not test any return-to-play criteria."
 }
}

112	                                                                                                                                    31   Abstract
113	
114	                                                                                                                                   32   Background
115	
116	                                                                                                                                   33   The anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) plays an important sensory role within the sensorimotor
117	
118	                                                                                                                                   34   system. Following ACL injury, sensorimotor dysfunction can have implications for rehabilitation and
119	
120	                                                                                                                                   35   risk of reinjury.

123	                                                                                                                                   36   Clinical question
124	
125	                                                                                                                                   37   What dysfunction occurs within the sensorimotor system following ACL injury, and how can

134	                                                                                                                                   39   Key results
135	
136	                                                                                                                                   40   Following ACL injury, dysfunction occurs across the sensorimotor system: afferent pathways, efferent
137	
138	                                                                                                                                   41   pathways and central processing. The afferent pathways exhibit dysfunction within the
139

142

145

147	
148	                                                                                                                                   44   reliance and central cortical processing). The efferent pathways have reduced excitability of the
149	
150	                                                                                                                                   45   central cortex, reduced descending motor pathway excitability and altered spinal reflexive excitability
151

163	
164	                                                                                                                                   50   accessible to clinicians. A practical approach to quantify the extent of sensorimotor dysfunction could
165

167

169

194	                                                                                                                                    58   Introduction
195	                                                                                                                                   59   The sensorimotor system is complex, and a central element of the body’s motor control system that
196	
197	                                                                                                                                   60   assists with planning and executing movement.82 It encompasses the afferent sensory systems, the
198	
199	                                                                                                                                   61   efferent motor pathways and the processing within the central cortex.82 The afferent sensory systems
200	
201	                                                                                                                                   62   include: visual, somatosensory (interpreting sensations from the skin and within the body such as pain,
202	
203	                                                                                                                                   63   touch and vibration), vestibular (balance and spatial orientation), olfactory, gustation and auditory
204	
205	                                                                                                                                   64   systems.55,76 Integrating sensory information from afferent systems, especially the somatosensory
206	
207	                                                                                                                                   65   and visual systems, allows the individual to gain accurate information from the environment to guide
208	
209	
210	
211	
212	Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®
213	                                                                                                                                   66   an appropriate movement strategy (Figure 1). The efferent motor pathways then signal the muscles
214	
215	                                                                                                                                   67   to execute the desired movement strategy.

231	
232	                                                                                                                                        sensorimotor cortex create an appropriate motor response.
233	                                                                                                                                    68   Musculoskeletal injuries, including anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injuries, lead to sensorimotor
234	
235	                                                                                                                                   69   system changes, and ultimately sensorimotor dysfunction.27,33,40,57,61 The dysfunction manifests as
236	
237	                                                                                                                                   70   errors in planning and executing movement.94 Sensorimotor dysfunction following ACL reconstruction
238	
239	                                                                                                                                   71   (ACLR) may be a risk factor in sustaining a new ACL injury,28,94 even after completing rehabilitation.
240	
241	                                                                                                                                   72   Therefore, clinicians must understand how sensorimotor dysfunction occurs following ACL injury, how
242	
243	                                                                                                                                   73   to assess it and rehabilitate it.
244	
245	
246	                                                                                                                                   74   This clinical commentary outlines sensorimotor changes following an ACL injury, and proposes
247	
248	                                                                                                                                   75   evidence-based methods to identify dysfunction, that are driven by our clinical practice. In part 2, we

257	                                                                                                                                   77   Clinical Question
258	
259	                                                                                                                                   78   What sensorimotor dysfunction occurs following ACL injury and how can clinicians assess it? The ACL
260	
261	                                                                                                                                   79   has two important roles: (1) providing structural knee stability by limiting excessive anterior
262	
263	
264	
265	
266	Downloaded from www.jospt.org at Ohio State University on May 21, 2025. For personal use only. No other uses without permission.
267	                                                                                                                                   80   translation and internal rotation of the tibia, and knee valgus,11,89 and (2) providing sensory
268	
269	                                                                                                                                   81   information to the sensorimotor cortex to facilitate motor planning and execution.22,68 Even when
270	
271	                                                                                                                                   82   structural stability is restored after ACLR, sensorimotor dysfunction remains,24,27 which may impair
272	
273	                                                                                                                                   83   gathering sensorimotor information from the environment when planning movement. Alterations in
274	
275	                                                                                                                                   84   efferent motor pathways remain following ACLR, even up to two years post-surgery with reduced
276

279	
280	Copyright © ${year} Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®. All rights reserved.
281	                                                                                                                                   85   strength and activation of the quadriceps.31,35
282	
283	
284	                                                                                                                                   86   Clinicians may lack either the clinical tools to identify individuals with sensorimotor dysfunction, or
285	
286	                                                                                                                                   87   rehabilitation methods may be inadequate. Dysfunction in the sensorimotor system following ACLR is
287	
288	                                                                                                                                   88   the same as for ACL injuries that are managed non-operatively and therefore, the two conditions
289	
290	                                                                                                                                   89   (ACLR and ACL injuries) are not separated.
291	                                                                                                                                     90   How does sensorimotor dysfunction impact movements?
292	                                                                                                                                    91   Motor planning and execution is complex. Neurocognitive demands (processing sensory, motor,
293	
294	                                                                                                                                    92   emotional and higher executive information) are increased in sporting situations due to movement
295	
296	                                                                                                                                    93   speed, greater decision-making complexity and reduced decision-making time. An athlete’s
297	
298	                                                                                                                                    94   movement strategy is determined by their constraints (anthropometrics and neuromuscular
299	
300	                                                                                                                                    95   capacities), the perceived environment information (opposition position and movement) and task
301	
302	                                                                                                                                    96   constraints (e.g. attempting to score a goal).2,12,102 Perception of environmental information and action
303	
304	                                                                                                                                    97   continuously occurs,20 requiring the athlete to integrate sensory information to generate an
305	
306	
307	
308	
309	Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®
310	                                                                                                                                    98   appropriate movement strategy. Individuals have several sensory systems: visual, somatosensory
311	
312	                                                                                                                                    99   (interpreting sensations from the skin and within the body such as pain, touch and vibration),
313	
314	                                                                                                                                   100   vestibular (balance and spatial orientation), olfactory (smell), gustation (taste) and auditory
315	
316	                                                                                                                                   101   (hearing),55,76 with the somatosensory and visual systems being the most pertinent for motor planning
317	
318	                                                                                                                                   102   and execution. Therefore, sensorimotor dysfunction can increase neurocognitive demands or reduce
319	
320	
321	
322

324	                                                                                                                                   103   the ability to plan high impact movements efficiently (such as cutting or jumping/landing).

327	                                                                                                                                   104   Key results
328	                                                                                                                                   105   Somatosensory system
329	                                                                                                                                   106   The somatosensory system (1) informs the central cortex about the position and movement of body
330	
331	                                                                                                                                   107   segments (proprioception) and, (2) senses painful and pressure/vibration stimuli.76 Proprioception
332	
333	
334	
335	
336	Copyright © ${year} Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®. All rights reserved.
337	                                                                                                                                   108   uses fast velocity afferent fibres (within muscle, ligament and joint tissue) to provide starting posture
338	
339	                                                                                                                                   109   information so that appropriate coordination of motor units can be produced to execute a
340	
341	                                                                                                                                   110   movement.75 The second somatosensory function uses soft tissue pain and pressure receptors to
342	
343	                                                                                                                                   111   detect pain or swelling so that if an injury occurs or tissue damage is imminent, then the body can
344	
345	                                                                                                                                   112   coordinate a motor response to minimise damage or protect the injured structure.81,86
346	
347	
348	                                                                                                                                   113   A full-thickness ACL tear results in a complete loss of mechanoreceptors.14 The return of these
349	
350	                                                                                                                                   114   mechanoreceptors following ACLR is often slow and variable,14 which may lead to altered
351	
352	                                                                                                                                   115   somatosensory processing and a reorganisation of the sensorimotor cortex with greater reliance being
353	                                                                                                                                    116   placed on the visual system.57 Diminished proprioceptive ability following ACLR may mean greater
354	
355	                                                                                                                                   117   error for the athlete when determining how their body is positioned in the environment. Knee
356	
357	                                                                                                                                   118   proprioception is reduced after ACLR, compared to both the uninjured limb and healthy control limbs,
358	
359	                                                                                                                                   119   even after rehabilitation and return to sport.42,79,80 Changes in surgical technique to preserve the
360	
361	                                                                                                                                   120   remnants of the ACL during reconstructive surgery may improve proprioception,7 but the surgical
362	
363	                                                                                                                                   121   technique is uncommon.
364	
365	
366	                                                                                                                                   122   Pain and swelling following an ACL injury may inhibit quadriceps activation.81 Knee joint effusion
367	
368	                                                                                                                                   123   causes activation of afferent pressure receptors within the joint capsule60 due to high intra-articular
369	
370	
371	
372	
373	Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®
374	                                                                                                                                   124   pressures, and chemical activation of the receptors due to inflammatory cytokines.81 Afferent pressure
375	
376	                                                                                                                                   125   receptor activations may reduce quadriceps activity64 and strength. 53 Similarly, pain and inflammation
377	
378	                                                                                                                                   126   can sensitise afferent receptors within the joint capsule and connective tissues, leading to further
379	
380	                                                                                                                                   127   quadriceps inhibition,60,81 with strength losses of 80-90% within the first few days following knee
381	
382	                                                                                                                                   128   surgery, which may persist in the weeks after.87 It is therefore essential to measure and monitor
383

388	                                                                                                                                   129   athlete pain and effusion throughout the rehabilitation process.

392	
393	                                                                                                                                   130   Assessment
394	                                                                                                                                   131   Assessing somatosensory function involves assessing somatosensory cortical processing demands,
395	
396	                                                                                                                                   132   assessing proprioception, and assessing pain and effusion (Table 1). However, the former generally
397

402	                                                                                                                                   133   uses equipment (e.g. functional brain MRI) not readily accessible. Therefore, clinicians should focus
403	
404	                                                                                                                                   134   on assessing proprioception, pain and effusion.

406

408	                                                                                                                                   136   Examining proprioceptive function is difficult because it covers several domains: (1) joint position
409
