                                      Serial Ultrasonography for the
                                      Assessment of Healing of Lower Extremity
                                      Bone Stress Injury and Correlation With
                                      Return to Sport/Exercise
                                      Brett G. Toresdahl, MD,†* Justin Conway, MD,‡ Theodore T. Miller, MD,§
                                      Marci A. Goolsby, MD,|| Christian S. Geannette, MD,§ Brianna Quijano, MS,¶
                                      and Lisa R. Callahan, MD||


                                      Background: Lower extremity bone stress injuries (BSIs) are common among athletes who participate in high-impact
                                      activities. Conventional imaging is limited in assessing healing of BSIs.
                                      Hypothesis: Serial ultrasonography (US) can identify changes in appearance of lower extremity BSIs over time that can be
                                      correlated with symptoms and return to exercise/sport.
                                      Study Design: Cohort observational study.
                                      Level of Evidence: Level 3.
                                      Methods: Adults 18 to 50 years old with a recent exercise-associated BSI of distal tibia/fibula or metatarsals diagnosed
                                      by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) were enrolled. US was performed every 2 weeks for 12 weeks. The sonographic
                                      appearance (soft tissue edema, periosteal reaction, hyperemia on power Doppler, callus) was correlated with the numerical
                                      rating scale (NRS) for pain and ability to return to sport/exercise.
                                      Results: A total of 30 patients were enrolled (mean age, 35.3 ± 7.7 years; 21 [70.0%] female). The tibia was most frequently
                                      affected (n = 15, 50.0%), followed by metatarsals (n = 14, 46.7%) and fibula (n = 1, 3.3%). At week 4, 25 of 30 (83.3%) had
                                      at least 1 US finding associated with the BSI. The degree of hyperemia was correlated with NRS at weeks 4 and 6 (Spearman
                                      correlations [ρ] 0.45 [0.09, 0.69] and 0.42 [0.07, 0.67], respectively), as well as return to sport/exercise at week 6 (ρ -0.45
                                      [-0.68, -0.09]). US soft tissue edema was also correlated with NRS at week 6 (ρ 0.38 [0.02, 0.65]).
                                      Conclusion: Serial US of lower extremity BSIs can provide objective measures of healing. US findings were correlated with
                                      clinical outcomes at multiple timepoints.
                                      Clinical Relevance: US may have advantages over conventional imaging for monitoring healing of lower extremity BSIs.
                                      Further research is needed to better understand the prognostic value of these sonographic indicators of BSI healing and role
                                      in assessing readiness for return to sport/exercise.
                                      Keywords: bone stress injury; magnetic resonance imaging; return to play; ultrasonography

 "evidenceSummary":"Prospective observational cohort of adults aged 18 to 50 with an exercise-related lower-leg or metatarsal bone stress injury confirmed by MRI, followed with ultrasound every two weeks for 12 weeks; 30 patients were analysed (mean age 35.3 years, 70% female, 90% running-related). Soft tissue edema and power Doppler hyperemia fell significantly over 12 weeks, and hyperemia correlated with pain at weeks 4 and 6 (rho 0.45 and 0.42) and with lower return-to-sport ratings at week 6 (rho -0.45).    "doi":"10.1177/19417381241231590",
   "abstract":"Prospective observational cohort of adults aged 18 to 50 with an MRI-confirmed exercise-related bone stress injury of the distal tibia, fibula or metatarsals. Serial ultrasound every two weeks for 12 weeks was correlated with pain (NRS) and return-to-sport ratings. Soft tissue edema and hyperemia decreased over time; hyperemia correlated with pain at weeks 4 and 6 and with return to sport at week 6.",
   "tldr":"Ultrasound of lower-leg and foot stress injuries showed edema and hyperemia fading over 12 weeks, and hyperemia tracked pain and return-to-sport ratings around weeks 4 to 6. The correlations are weak and the study is small, so ultrasound looks promising for monitoring but is not a return-to-sport test yet.",
   "methods":"Adults aged 18 to 50 with a recent exercise-related distal tibia, fibula or metatarsal bone stress injury confirmed by MRI were enrolled within four weeks of MRI and scanned every two weeks for 12 weeks. Two blinded musculoskeletal radiologists scored soft tissue edema, periosteal reaction, hyperemia (0 to 3) and callus. Patients completed pain (NRS) and return-to-sport surveys biweekly, and MRI was repeated at 12 weeks. Repeated-measures ANOVA, paired t tests and Spearman correlations were used.",
   "findings":"Of 31 enrolled, 30 were analysed. Soft tissue edema, periosteal reaction and hyperemia were observed in 66.7%, 63.3% and 43.3% of patients at baseline (ultrasound). Soft tissue edema fell from 0.95 at week 2 to 0.34 at week 12 and hyperemia from 0.63 to 0.07 (both P < .01); periosteal reaction did not change significantly (P = .23). Hyperemia correlated with average pain at week 4 (rho 0.45, 95% CI 0.09 to 0.69) and week 6 (rho 0.42, 95% CI 0.07 to 0.67), and with return to sport at week 6 (rho -0.45, 95% CI -0.68 to -0.09). Soft tissue edema correlated with pain at week 6 (rho 0.38). MRI marrow edema fell from 1.3 to 0.79 (P < .01), but it persisted in 53.3% at 12 weeks and did not correlate with pain or return to sport.",
   "limitations":"Single centre, no comparison group, small sample, and a 4-point subjective ultrasound scale with inter-observer variability. The return-to-sport scale was not validated, most patients had not fully returned by week 12, and no correlations were significant after week 6. The abstract says 30 patients were enrolled, but the Results say 31 were enrolled and one was excluded after week 2. Table 1 gives metatarsal 49.7% while the text gives 46.7%.",
   "practicalImplications":"Ultrasound every two weeks could track hyperemia and soft tissue edema alongside symptoms, which may help where repeat MRI is less useful. The authors note athletic training rooms may be able to use it, but the findings support clinical judgment rather than replacing it.",
   "athleteDev":"Not a performance application. Staff who manage progression after a bone stress injury could look at the trend in hyperemia and symptoms, but the study does not test load or training decisions.",
   "rtp":"Hyperemia at week 6 was associated with lower return-to-sport ratings, so it may be a useful added signal. The paper cannot set a clearance threshold: correlations were weak, the return-to-sport scale was not validated, and no prognostic cut-off was derived."
